name: Recency illusion
statement: Someone who notices a word or a construction for the first time takes it to be new, and the form is usually much older than that.
meaning: The claim is about age, not about rate. Zwicky's 2006 wording is "If you've noticed something only recently, you believe that it originated recently." He named it for language, and every example he gives is a form that a speaker or a writer dates to the last twenty or thirty years. Checking it takes two dates. The first is the date somebody asserts for a form's arrival, which has to be written down somewhere before anyone can hold it to account. The second is the date the form actually appears in the record, which historical dictionaries and text corpora supply. That second date is why this illusion is cheaper to test than most of the ideas in this atlas. It is also why the testing done so far covers published claims about language rather than what a person privately believes.

origin.note: Zwicky introduced the Recency Illusion and the Frequency Illusion in one post, 'Just between Dr. Language and I', which he describes as a lightly edited version of a message sent to the American Dialect Society mailing list that day. A follow-up on 17 August added the Adolescent Illusion and the Out-Group Illusion. His fullest statement is the abstract 'Why are we so illuded?', dated September 2006, which sets out five illusions and traces them to Language Log postings of the previous two years. Neither text reports a measurement.

evidence: The 2005 post answers a usage columnist at yourdictionary.com who wrote that American speakers began switching 'me and X' to 'X and I' in every position about 20 years earlier. James Cochrane's book Between You and I dates the same shift to the previous twenty or so years. Zwicky replies from the Oxford English Dictionary and Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage. The rise of 'between you and I' in Late Modern English goes back at least 150 or 160 years, and earlier uses go back about 400. His second case is a linguist rather than a columnist. Charles Hockett called 'I'm going home and eat' a recent colloquial pattern in 1958, and David Denison had collected examples from roughly 30 years before that. The follow-up post adds retro-'not', which people report as recent and as teenage speech, and cites Larry Horn's 1992 paper against both impressions. The 2006 abstract supplies a mechanism, and it is not the one the 2005 post gives. There Zwicky assigns selective attention and confirmation bias to the Frequency Illusion, and says that in the Recency and Out-Group Illusions a feature is salient because it is judged bad, innovation being read as laziness, ignorance and putting on airs. Neither text counts anything. The term reached peer review two years later. Rickford, Buchstaller, Wasow and Zwicky apply it in American Speech to Waksler's treatment of intensifier 'all' as new, and set against it examples from Aelfric's Lives of Saints dated 990 and 1000. The one quantitative survey located is van der Meulen's, on Dutch prescriptive writing. He searched a database of 5,678 entries from publications dated 1900 to 2018. Of those, 238 entries carry at least one recency statement, and they target 341 usage items, 230 of them lexical and 98 grammatical. Claims about recent origins, the strictly Zwickian kind, account for 80.9% of statements, or 276. He dated the forms against four historical dictionaries and against Delpher, a repository of over 120 million pages of Dutch newspapers, books and magazines. A form first attested more than 30 years before the statement counted as an illusion, a threshold taken from Zwicky's Hockett example. Sampling was random, at most two lexical and two grammatical items per decade. Of the 23 lexical recency statements checked, 20 are illusions, 87%, and three are not. For 17 of them the earliest occurrence predates the claim by more than 50 years. Thirteen grammatical statements across eight usage items are almost all illusions, with the relative pronoun 'wat' rated a maybe.

replication.headline: No replication was located, and there is no original experiment to repeat: the effect was named in a blog post that measures nothing.
replication.detail: The one quantitative test found, van der Meulen's survey of Dutch prescriptive publications, supports the claim at 20 illusions in 23 lexical statements. That is a first test rather than a repeat. It covers one language, one genre and a sample of at most two items per decade, and no attempt to run the same design elsewhere was located. Its author calls his own 30-year cut-off arbitrary and warns that frequency terms may not carry across languages. Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar for the phrase returned that paper and no psychological experiment on it.

limits: The searches behind this verdict covered Crossref by bibliographic query, Europe PMC full-text search, Semantic Scholar by phrase and by title, the papers citing van der Meulen at Semantic Scholar, and web searches for experimental tests under the name. Europe PMC returned a single hit, on meningioma surgery. The citation list returned four papers, none of them a repeat of the design. One OpenAlex query was refused by the service and was not retried. What has been tested is narrow in a way the headline figure hides. Van der Meulen counts what prescriptive authors published, not what ordinary speakers believe, and he says his results are not evidence that all language users are always wrong. He excluded claims about new meanings of existing wordforms and claims about a recent rise in frequency, so the 23 statements are the subset that could be dated at all. His own reporting does not sit flush: the sentence carrying the result calls them '17 lexical usage items' while giving 20 of 23 statements as illusions, and the table below it lists the items with their years. The three exceptions are mond-aan-mondreclame at six years, hoogspanning at 25 and mentaliteit at exactly 30, and he notes that belevenis at 34 years is an illusion only by the width of his threshold. That paper was read as the PDF deposited in Radboud University's repository, because the publisher's own site refused every request made here. Graves's 2024 Journal of Pragmatics article on the rise of so-prefacing is paywalled and was not read; what appears here comes from the abstract of her later article in Publication of the American Dialect Society, read at Crossref. Zwicky's 2006 abstract was read from the PDF on his Stanford page and was not traced to a published proceedings. The Oxford English Dictionary's current treatment of the phrase was not inspected, because the dictionary is paywalled.
misreadings: Three separate things share a word. The recency illusion is about the age of a form. The frequency illusion, named in the same post, is about how often the form occurs. The recency effect in memory is about the last items in a list being recalled best, and recency bias in investment writing is a claim about weighting new information. Showing that 'between you and I' is 400 years old settles the first and touches none of the others. Zwicky's mechanism travels as though it were a result. Wikipedia's article says the illusion is caused by selective attention and cites the 2005 post, which does say exactly that. The 2006 abstract routes the Recency Illusion elsewhere, through a language ideology that reads innovation as laziness, and reserves selective attention and confirmation bias for the Frequency Illusion. Both accounts are Zwicky's own, offered without data, and they disagree. The Dutch result is not a licence to dismiss any claim of novelty. Three of 23 lexical statements were accurate, and the line between accurate and illusory is a 30-year threshold its author calls arbitrary. Zwicky's own co-authored paper makes the point more sharply. Intensifier 'all' goes back to Old English, so calling it new was an illusion. Quotative 'all', as in 'he's all, why don't you ever do what you're told', did start in California in the early 1980s. The earliest report the authors found is the autumn 1982 issue of the newsletter Not Just Words. Graves reports that so-prefacing, widely perceived as new, has tentatively been found to be rising since the 1990s. A form that feels new is sometimes new. What the illusion supplies is the confidence, not the evidence. The last error is status. Frequency illusion entered the Oxford English Dictionary in the March 2019 batch of updates; Ben Zimmer noted at the time that recency illusion had not, and a commenter on that post remarked on the asymmetry. Being in a dictionary records that people use a phrase, and measures nothing about the thing it names.

sources.text: Zwicky, A. (2005). Just between Dr. Language and I. Language Log, 7 August 2005. The post that coined 'Recency Illusion' and 'Frequency Illusion'; a blog post, not a peer-reviewed venue.
Zwicky, A. (2005). More illusions. Language Log, 17 August 2005. Restates both illusions, adds the Adolescent and Out-Group Illusions, and gives the retro-'not' example.
Zwicky, A. M. (2006). Why are we so illuded? Abstract dated September 2006, hosted at Stanford University as LSA07illude.abst.pdf. Defines the Recency Illusion as one of five and gives its mechanism.

Rickford, J. R., Buchstaller, I., Wasow, T., & Zwicky, A. (2007). Intensive and quotative all: Something old, something new. American Speech, 82(1), 3-31. Read in full from the copy hosted on Thomas Wasow's Stanford page. Uses the term in print and dates both functions of 'all'.

van der Meulen, M. (2022). Are we indeed so illuded? Recency and frequency illusions in Dutch prescriptivism. Languages, 7(1), 42. Read in full from the PDF in Radboud University's repository; the publisher's site refused access.

Graves, S. It drives me mad seeing people answer questions with so: Overt and covert attitudes toward so-prefacing answers. Publication of the American Dialect Society, 110(1), 127-149. The abstract, read at Crossref, is the source for so-prefacing having been tentatively found to be on the rise since the 1990s.

Graves, S. (2024). New use of an old discourse marker: The rise of prefacing answers to questions with so. Journal of Pragmatics, 225, 69-86. Paywalled and not read; the record was verified at Crossref and nothing from the paper is quoted here.
Zimmer, B. (2019). "Frequency illusion" in the OED. Language Log, 19 March 2019. Records that the OED took frequency illusion in its March 2019 updates and that recency illusion had not entered.
Wikipedia, Recency illusion. Read for what it claims rather than relied on as evidence; the source of the widely repeated statement that Zwicky attributed the illusion to selective attention.
